extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and general readers interested in theatre history and Restoration-era drama
extracted.subtask_description: Features, conventions, themes and stage-practices that define Restoration comedy (English stage comedy c.1660–1710), useful for identifying, analyzing, or producing plays in the genre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy of manners / genre label
rubrics_metrics.description: Restoration comedy is English comedy written and performed in the Restoration period of 1660–1710; 'comedy of manners' is used as a synonym.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat works in this period as part of the comedy-of-manners tradition: emphasis on social behavior, wit, and the mores of a particular social class rather than plot-driven moralizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexual frankness / sexually explicit language
rubrics_metrics.description: Sexually explicit language was encouraged by King Charles II and the rakish style of his court; dramatists 'gloried in it and intended to shock those who did not like it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect frank references, bawdy jokes, and deliberate attempts to shock. Example: Wycherley's The Country Wife and its 'China scene' rely on sustained double entendre implying off-stage sex.

rubrics_metrics.name: Up-to-the-minute topicality
rubrics_metrics.description: Plays attracted audiences by up-to-the-minute topical writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inclusion of contemporary references, fashions and news was a selling point—audiences valued topical jokes and current-event allusions that could date a play quickly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crowded, bustling multi-plot action
rubrics_metrics.description: Audiences demanded bustling, crowded multi-plot action and fast pace; variety within a single play was prized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plays often combine several interlinked plots (e.g., Love in a Tub mixes heroic conflict, urbane wit, and burlesque). Avoid structurally simple single-plot comedies if aiming for a Restoration style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of stock character-types: rake and fop
rubrics_metrics.description: Prominent character-types include the Restoration rake (sexually irresistible aristocratic libertine) and the fop; the rake is a central template (e.g., Dorimant in The Man of Mode).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characterization often celebrates or satirically depicts aristocratic sexual conquest and fashionable vice; the rake drives many seduction plots and intrigues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wit, wordplay, and double entendre
rubrics_metrics.description: Witty dialogue, 'wit duels' between lovers, and extensive double entendre are central features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect fast verbal sparring, clever retorts, and set-piece scenes of verbal combat (e.g., prenuptial debates like the 'Proviso' scene in The Way of the World).

rubrics_metrics.name: Breeches roles and the first professional actresses
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduction of professional actresses changed stage dynamics; breeches roles (women in male clothes) were common and displayed the actress's body and freedom of behaviour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Casting women in male dress was used for comic and erotic effect and could be read as either subverting gender roles or objectifying actresses; about a quarter of plays (1660–1700) contain breeches roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Star/celebrity actor culture
rubrics_metrics.description: Actors became the first public celebrities; audiences were often drawn by performances of specific actors rather than authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Productions and plays could be tailored to showcase celebrity performers (benefit nights, company shares, star deals). Charisma and delivery could be as important as text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stagecraft and theatre design
rubrics_metrics.description: Theatres featured apron/thrust stages, moveable scenery, elaborate machines for effects, music and dancing—designed for intimate audience contact and spectacle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Staging conventions (apron stage, machinery, music/dance) supported close actor–audience interaction and could be exploited for physical comedy, spectacle, or risqué business.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixing genres and variety (burlesque, heroic elements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Restoration plays commonly mix tones and genres—burlesque, heroic verse scenes, and classical borrowings appear alongside witty comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Genre-mixing within a single play (incongruous tone shifts) was accepted and even valued by contemporary audiences; modern producers should preserve variety rather than homogenize tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot devices: imposture, tricks, forged letters
rubrics_metrics.description: Common devices include imposture (e.g., Horner's impotence trick), false rumours, forged letters and near-discoveries that drive comic complications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These mechanisms create dramatic irony and situation comedy; expect repeated near-revelations and clever evasions rather than moral reformation of rakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fast fashion changes / rapid evolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Fashions in drama changed almost week by week; the genre evolved quickly and varied by decade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 'Restoration' play may look very different depending on date (e.g., 1670s 'aristocratic' comedies vs softer 1690s plays aimed at mixed audiences). Historical sensitivity to sub-period matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience composition and shifting targets
rubrics_metrics.description: Early audiences were socially diverse (aristocrats, servants, middle-class); by the 1690s playwrights aimed at more socially mixed and female spectators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tone and subject-matter shift depending on intended audience—aristocratic, hard-edged wit for courtly taste vs softened marriage-focused themes for middle-class and female viewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Talk plays / emphasis on discussion
rubrics_metrics.description: Some Restoration plays (e.g., The Provoked Wife) are 'talk plays' that focus on discussions, moral or legal complexity and witty debates rather than on action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect extended conversational scenes and debate; successful productions must sustain verbal energy and character interplay rather than physical spectacle alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shift toward marital themes in later period
rubrics_metrics.description: In the 1690s comedies moved the war between the sexes into marriage and focused more on marital relations after the wedding bells.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Later Restoration comedy often centers on prenuptial negotiations, marital satire, and the social/legal realities of married women (separation, maintenance), requiring attention to domestic and legal context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tolerance and censorship context
rubrics_metrics.description: Public tolerance for sexual frankness waned by century's end; attacks (e.g., Jeremy Collier) and the Society for the Reformation of Manners prosecuted playwrights, reducing permissiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider historical and social constraints: provocative content risked moral backlash, legal action, and changing patronage; producers/writers balancing authenticity and acceptability must be aware of shifting norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial and managerial pressures shaping content
rubrics_metrics.description: Company competition, patent theatres, monopolies, and management (e.g., Rich, cooperative companies) strongly influenced which plays were produced and how they catered to audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Economic context (need for box-office success, ten-performance benchmark) encouraged topicality, spectacle, or pandering to public taste; practical production choices often reflect commercial imperatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone spectrum: 'hard' (unsentimental) vs 'soft' comedies
rubrics_metrics.description: Restoration comedy spans a tone spectrum: 'unsentimental or "hard" comedies' (e.g., Dryden, Wycherley) celebrating aristocratic vice, versus 'softer' later comedies (e.g., Congreve, Vanbrugh) with more humane characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When classifying or writing in the mode, place a play on this spectrum—harsh, satirical exposure of vice vs subtler, marriage-oriented, audience-friendly wit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical reception and later adaptation practice
rubrics_metrics.description: From the 18th–19th centuries plays were often heavily adapted or bowdlerised due to sexual frankness; modern revival requires decisions about faithfulness vs adaptation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholars and producers should note that many canonical plays survive in altered forms; staging originals may require careful editing or contextual framing for contemporary audiences.
